Point $P$ is a moving point on this line. Through point $P$, $PM$ is drawn perpendicular to the $x$-axis at point $M$, and $PN$ is drawn perpendicular to the $y$-axis at point $N$. On quadrilateral $PMON$, the following segments are intercepted: $PC=\frac{1}{3}MP$, $MB=\frac{1}{3}OM$, $OE=\frac{1}{3}ON$, and $ND=\frac{1}{3}NP$. Quadrilateral $BCDE$ is a parallelogram. Is there such a point $P$ on the line $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+b$ that makes quadrilateral $BCDE$ a square? If such a point exists, please find the coordinates of all such points $P$; if it does not exist, please explain why.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} Let the coordinates of point $P$ be $(x,y)$,

when $\triangle OBE \cong \triangle MCB$, quadrilateral $BCDE$ becomes a square,

$OE=BM$,

when point $P$ is in the first quadrant, i.e., $\frac{1}{3}y=\frac{1}{3}x$, $x=y$.

Point $P$ lies on the line,

$\left\{\begin{array}{l}
y=\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\
y=x
\end{array}\right.$,

solving we get $\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x=\boxed{2} \\
y=2
\end{array}\right.$,

when point $P$ is in the second quadrant, $-x=y$

$\left\{\begin{array}{l}
y=\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\
y=-x
\end{array}\right.$,

solving we get $\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x=-6 \\
y=6
\end{array}\right.$

There exists such a point $P$ on the line $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+b$ that makes quadrilateral $BCDE$ a square, with $P$'s coordinates being $\boxed{(2,2)}$ or $\boxed{(-6,6)}$.

raw_record.original_question: As shown in the figure, it is known that the graph of the linear function $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+b$ passes through point $A(0,3)$. Point $P$ is a moving point on this line. Through point $P$, $PM$ is drawn perpendicular to the $x$-axis at point $M$, and $PN$ is drawn perpendicular to the $y$-axis at point $N$. On quadrilateral $PMON$, the following segments are intercepted: $PC=\frac{1}{3}MP$, $MB=\frac{1}{3}OM$, $OE=\frac{1}{3}ON$, and $ND=\frac{1}{3}NP$. Quadrilateral $BCDE$ is a parallelogram. Is there such a point $P$ on the line $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+b$ that makes quadrilateral $BCDE$ a square? If such a point exists, please find the coordinates of all such points $P$; if it does not exist, please explain why.
raw_record.answer:
Solution: Let the coordinates of point $P$ be $(x,y)$.

When $\triangle OBE \cong \triangle MCB$, quadrilateral $BCDE$ becomes a square, so $OE=BM$.

When point $P$ is in the first quadrant, i.e., $\frac{1}{3}y=\frac{1}{3}x$, then $x=y$.

Point $P$ lies on the line,
$\left\{\begin{array}{l}
y=\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\
y=x
\end{array}\right.$,
so solving gives $\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x=2 \\
y=2
\end{array}\right.$.

When point $P$ is in the second quadrant, $-x=y$.

$\left\{\begin{array}{l}
y=\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\
y=-x
\end{array}\right.$,
so solving gives $\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x=-6 \\
y=6
\end{array}\right.$.

Therefore, there exists such a point $P$ on the line $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+b$ that makes quadrilateral $BCDE$ a square, with coordinates $P=(2,2)$ or $P=(-6,6)$.

ready3_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, it is known that the graph of the linear function $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+b$ passes through point $A(0,3)$. Point $P$ is a moving point on this line. Through point $P$, $PM$ is drawn perpendicular to the $x$-axis at point $M$, and $PN$ is drawn perpendicular to the $y$-axis at point $N$. On quadrilateral $PMON$, the following segments are intercepted: $PC=\frac{1}{3}MP$, $MB=\frac{1}{3}OM$, $OE=\frac{1}{3}ON$, and $ND=\frac{1}{3}NP$. Quadrilateral $BCDE$ is a parallelogram. Is there such a point $P$ on the line $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+b$ that makes quadrilateral $BCDE$ a square? If such a point exists, please find the coordinates of all such points $P$; if it does not exist, please explain why.
ready3_open_rewrite.raw_answer:
Solution: Let the coordinates of point $P$ be $(x,y)$.

When $\triangle OBE \cong \triangle MCB$, quadrilateral $BCDE$ becomes a square, so $OE=BM$.

When point $P$ is in the first quadrant, i.e., $\frac{1}{3}y=\frac{1}{3}x$, then $x=y$.

Point $P$ lies on the line,
$\left\{\begin{array}{l}
y=\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\
y=x
\end{array}\right.$,
so solving gives $\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x=2 \\
y=2
\end{array}\right.$.

When point $P$ is in the second quadrant, $-x=y$.

$\left\{\begin{array}{l}
y=\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\
y=-x
\end{array}\right.$,
so solving gives $\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x=-6 \\
y=6
\end{array}\right.$.

Therefore, there exists such a point $P$ on the line $y=-\frac{1}{2}x+b$ that makes quadrilateral $BCDE$ a square, with coordinates $P=(2,2)$ or $P=(-6,6)$.
